title: Online engagement with 2020 election misinformation and turnout in the 2021 Georgia runoff election
screen_reason: The paper's aim is the association between engagement with 2020 election-fraud conspiracy content and turnout, but the Fig. 1 caption reports a behavioural descriptive share with an explicit denominator: of 7,324 Georgia Twitter panel users active before and after the 2020 election, 558 liked or retweeted fraud-related content by promoters of conspiracy theories. That is a share of people who engaged with misinformation at least once, from platform data - eligible under the 'descriptive share reported anywhere' rule.

estimates.country: United States (registered voters in the state of Georgia)
estimates.date: Likes/retweets before and after the 3 November 2020 general election; the fraud-tweet corpus covers 23 October 2020 to 5 January 2021; turnout outcome is the 5 January 2021 Georgia runoff
estimates.measure_type: % of active Georgia Twitter panel users who liked or retweeted at least one election-fraud tweet posted by conspiracy-theory promoters
estimates.denominator: 7,324 Twitter users uniquely matched to Georgia voter-file records who liked and/or retweeted any content both before and after the 2020 general election (drawn from 45,431 voter-file-matched Georgians in a 1.5-million-voter Twitter panel)
estimates.definition: The user liked or retweeted at least one tweet that was (1) about election fraud and (2) posted by a user belonging to one of the four Twitter communities that Abilov et al. identified as promoting fraud conspiracy theories. Quote tweets were excluded; likes come from Twitter's 10% 'decahose' sample.
estimates.misinfo_def: "Republican elected officials, including then-President Donald Trump, promoted conspiracy theories claiming that Joe Biden's close victory in Georgia was fraudulent"; operationally, "we code users in our sample as endorsing fraud if they liked or retweeted a tweet in the user communities that promoted conspiracy theories. These tweets were 1) about election fraud and 2) tweeted by a user who was part of a community that, by and large, promoted conspiracy theories."
estimates.source_quote: Of the 7,324 Georgia Twitter users in the panel who were active both before and after the 2020 election, 558 liked or retweeted fraud-related content by promoters of conspiracy theories (228 of 974 superusers), and 1,071 liked or retweeted fraud-related content of detractors (489 of 974 superusers).
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Labels are inherited from Abilov et al. (5): fraud-related tweets identified with hand-curated keywords and hashtags ('voter fraud', '#voterfraud', '#stopthesteal' added 3 Nov 2020) with machine assistance for variants; stance assigned NOT by reading tweets but by Infomap community detection on the retweet network - five communities covering 90% of users were split into a four-community promoting cluster and a one-community detracting cluster. Validated indirectly against an independent survey (COVID States Project, 1,528 linked respondents): promoters had lower confidence in 2020 election fairness after controlling for partisanship and 2020 vote choice. Only 1% of the active sample was coded as both promoting and detracting.
estimates.moderator_quote: Fig. 1. Fraction of active users (any likes/retweets) in the Twitter panel that liked/retweeted fraud-related posts before and after the 2020 election.
estimates.notes: JUDGEMENT CALL on construct. The numerator is users who LIKED OR RETWEETED misinformation at least once and the denominator is people, so I coded REACH with reach_subtype=sharing (per the rule 'people reached >= 1, behavioural -> REACH', whose subtypes include sharing and liking), and denom_scope=population follows automatically. An adjudicator could equally defend SHARING with sharing_subtype=actor_share ('% of users who shared any'); the two codings are formally overlapping in the protocol. Note the measure mixes likes (a private signal, observed only through a 10% decahose sample) with retweets (public), so it UNDERSTATES engagement - the authors say so explicitly. classification_level=mixed because eligibility required both a content keyword match and the author's membership of a promoting community; ground_truth=classifier because the stance assignment is algorithmic (community detection), with no per-tweet human veracity judgement. value 7.62% is an exact part/whole share from two verbatim counts with the same denominator (558/7,324), per R8.

missed_or_uncertain: NOT EXTRACTED: (1) SUPERUSER SUBGROUP - 228 of 974 superusers (23.4%) liked or retweeted fraud-promoting content (superusers = users with 200+ likes/retweets in the period, the top 10% most active). It is a verbatim count pair with its own denominator, but it is an activity subgroup rather than the paper's headline, so it is not a row; an adjudicator wanting an activity moderator can add it. (2) 1,071/7,324 (14.6%) liked or retweeted fraud-related content by DETRACTORS (debunkers) - engagement with counter-misinformation content, not with misinformation. (3) 'only 1% of the active user sample coded one on both variables' - a share of users coded as both promoting and detracting; a data-quality figure, not a prevalence estimate. (4) 76% of the Republicans who provided a Twitter handle and publicly promoted election fraud conspiracies also agreed that 'Hydroxychloroquine is an effective treatment for coronavirus' (vs 34% of Republicans with Twitter handles) - this is BELIEF in a false claim, explicitly excluded by the protocol, and its denominator (a subset of 1,528 survey-linked respondents) is not stated. (5) '77% of Republicans reported that they believed there was widespread fraud' and '72% indicated that they did not trust that the results of the 2020 election were accurate' - both are figures the paper CITES from other sources (refs 47, 48), excluded per R8. (6) The friend/exposure analysis (39,381 users who followed any other users) reports regression coefficients only, no share exposed. (7) Sample-construction percentages (88% of 51,576 Georgia-matched users found in the voter file in both 2017 and 2020) are coverage figures, not misinformation shares. QUOTE CAVEAT: the text file for this paper interleaves the two printed PNAS columns on the same physical lines, so no multi-line sentence from the body text is a contiguous verbatim span. All quotes here are therefore taken either from the full-width Fig. 1 caption or from a single line of one column; the case-definition sentence in full reads 'In our analyses with these data, and following Abilov et al. (5), we code users in our sample as endorsing fraud if they liked or retweeted a tweet in the user communities that promoted conspiracy theories.' (Materials and Methods, Data), of which item6_quote quotes the one line that is contiguous in the file.

rob.design: Observational linkage of a Twitter panel to administrative records: 1.5 million registered voters name-matched to Twitter profiles in 2018 (Grinberg et al./Hughes et al. method), 51,576 uniquely linked in Georgia, 45,431 present in the Georgia voter file in both 2017 and 2020; Georgia voter file (23 Nov 2020) and voter history file (20 Jul 2021) give ground-truth turnout; TargetSmart 2017 supplies demographics and a proprietary partisan score (Georgia has no partisan registration). Misinformation exposure/engagement measured as likes (10% decahose sample) and retweets of tweets in the Abilov et al. fraud corpus (23 Oct 2020 - 5 Jan 2021), stance assigned by Infomap community detection, quote tweets excluded. Descriptive analyses restricted to 7,324 users active in both periods. Acknowledged limits: no per-tweet human veracity coding, likes only 10% sampled, cannot observe actual exposure, non-representative Twitter panel, observational design, voter file postdating the 2020 election may miss late registrants.
